description: Welcome to the Parish of Mickleham: St Michael and All Angels and Westhumble Chapel, a Christian community in the Surrey Hills.
content: St Michael & All Angels Church, with its blue clock, red door, churchyard and surrounding trees. Mickleham & Westhumble About our parish A welcoming church community serving the villages of Mickleham and Westhumble. Who we are A parish with a place for you Our parish brings together St Michael and All Angels in Mickleham and the Chapel of Ease in Westhumble. We are part of the Church of England and the United Benefice of Leatherhead and Mickleham, within the Diocese of Guildford. People from the villages and nearby towns form a friendly church community. We seek to care for one another through worship, spiritual support, practical help and encouragement. All are welcome to visit or join in parish life. Meet our two churches “Inspired by God’s love we seek to grow spiritually, make Jesus Christ known and be a loving, inclusive and welcoming church, at the heart of the community.” Our parish vision People gathering and talking inside St Michael & All Angels Church. title: Alpha Course
documentTitle: Alpha Course | St Michael & All Angels
description: A welcoming space to explore the basics of Christian faith, ask questions and share your point of view.
content: ← Our Community Explore faith Alpha Course A welcoming space to explore the basics of Christian faith, ask questions and share your point of view. What is Alpha? The parish describes Alpha as a series of sessions exploring the basics of Christian faith. It is for anyone who would like to explore, ask questions and share their point of view, whatever their background or context. What happens at a session? The format described by the parish begins with tea and cake, followed by a short film presentation on a question about Christian faith and time for discussion. The course material explores topics including Jesus, prayer, faith, the Holy Spirit, the Bible and how God guides us. Who is Alpha for? Alpha is intended for people who want space to explore Christian faith and ask questions. You do not need to have everything worked out before you come. Ask about a future course The old website listed a course contact and dates that may no longer be current, so no course date or named contact is shown here. title: Baptisms at St Michael & All Angels
documentTitle: Baptisms | St Michael & All Angels
description: A joyful welcome into the life of the Church. Enquiries are welcome for children and adults.
content: Illustrative baptismal font with sunlit water in a church interior. A journey of faith Baptisms at St Michael & All Angels A joyful welcome into the life of the Church. Enquiries are welcome for children and adults. Ask about a baptism Discover the baptism journey ↓ A joyful welcome A welcome into the life of the Church. Children & adults Enquiries are welcome at different stages of life. Belonging together Become connected to the worshipping life of the church. Growing in faith Preparation, worship and continuing support. A joyful beginning A significant step. A warm welcome. Baptism is a significant step in the Christian faith and marks a person’s welcome into the life of the Church. The parish welcomes enquiries for children and adults. Whether your enquiry is for a child or for yourself, begin by talking with the parish. Begin a conversation The baptism journey Taking the next step, together 1 Get in touch Initial enquiries and bookings are made through the parish clergy or parish baptism officer. 2 Talk about arrangements The clergy agree arrangements and decide how exceptional circumstances should be handled. 3 Prepare for baptism Candidates—and, for a child, their parents or carers—will be offered appropriate preparation. 4 Continue in church life After baptism, the church continues to welcome and support the person and their family. Illustrative close view of rippling baptismal water reflecting soft church light. At the font A welcome into Christian faith Baptism marks a person’s welcome into the life of the Church. Preparation helps those involved understand its meaning, the promises made in the service and its place in Christian faith. Useful information Making space for your questions The parish guidance below explains the practical details. Please talk to us about your circumstances. Who may be baptised? Under the parish policy agreed by the PCC in September 2026, baptism will normally be available to people who live in the parish, belong to the church, regularly worship here, are on the Electoral Roll, or have another recognised connection with the parish or church. The clergy may consider other requests where there is a strong pastoral reason and, where appropriate, may seek the consent of the candidate’s own parish priest or incumbent. Preparing for baptism Candidates—and, for a child, their parents or carers—will be offered appropriate preparation. This helps those involved understand the meaning of baptism, the promises made in the service and baptism’s place in Christian faith and the worshipping life of the church. Parents or carers should be able to make the promises with integrity. Godparents are welcome to take part in preparation where possible. Children and godparents Parents or carers take part in a child’s preparation and baptism service. Before a baptism is arranged, the parish expects the family to attend several church services to become familiar with and connected to the worshipping life of the church. Godparents are chosen by the parents or carers and must be baptised. The usual expectation is three godparents, ideally two of the same sex as the child; the minimum is two, and the policy suggests a maximum of six, with flexibility where appropriate. Someone who is not baptised may be included as a sponsor or may consider baptism before the service. Adults and older candidates Adults and older candidates receive preparation suited to their circumstances. Where appropriate, baptism may be linked with preparation for confirmation. Two or more sponsors may be chosen. When and where? Baptisms normally take place during the main Sunday morning service, usually the All-Age Worship service listed on the first Sunday of the month. Another time may be arranged for a good pastoral or practical reason, with the clergy’s agreement. In that case, the person baptised is expected to be welcomed at a main Sunday service on another occasion. Please check the Calendar for current service dates. Check the Calendar → Thanksgiving or blessing Where baptism is not possible, not desired or not yet the right step, the church may offer a service of thanksgiving or blessing. This provides an opportunity to give thanks, pray for the child or candidate and mark the occasion without the baptismal promises. Baptism Policy The parish policy agreed by the PCC in September 2026. Read the Baptism Policy (DOCX) ↗ Baptism Application Form The parish application form supplied for baptism enquiries. Download Baptism Application Form (PDF) ↗ St Michael and All Angels in Mickleham, with its blue clock, spire and red entrance door. Thinking about baptism? We would be delighted to hear from you Initial enquiries and bookings are made through the parish clergy or parish baptism officer. The clergy agree arrangements, ensure preparation takes place and decide how exceptional circumstances should be handled. After baptism, the church continues to welcome and support the person and their family through worship, teaching, pastoral care and appropriate information about church activities. title: Fellowship & Bible Study Groups
documentTitle: Fellowship & Bible Study Groups | St Michael & All Angels
description: Fellowship and Bible study groups are an important part of parish community life: a place to study the Bible, ask questions, share experiences and grow together.
content: ← Our Community Community & Faith Fellowship & Bible Study Groups Fellowship and Bible study groups are an important part of parish community life: a place to study the Bible, ask questions, share experiences and grow together. Growing together Learning, sharing and growing together In a safe, confidential and non-judgemental setting, people can explore faith together, learn, ask questions and take part in one another’s lives. Explore the Bible Study Scripture together and make space for personal discovery and spiritual growth. Ask questions Share thoughts openly and learn alongside others in a safe, confidential and non-judgemental environment. Share life Talk about the joys and challenges of being a Christian in society today, and share refreshments. Build friendships Smaller meetings help relationships to develop, strengthening a sense of community and belonging. Regular groups Meet during the week Two regular Bible study groups meet weekly in Westhumble. Everyone is welcome. Monday Monday Bible Study Group Time 7:45 pm Place Westhumble Thursday Thursday Bible Study Group Time 11:00 am Place Westhumble Everyone is welcome Come as you are New members are always welcome. You do not need to be an expert in the Bible or theology to join. These informal groups are a chance to study, ask questions, share refreshments and get to know one another better. At particular seasons Groups through the seasons At particular seasons in life and in the church calendar, shorter fixed-length groups may also meet. Find out more Interested in joining? Contact the parish office to ask about joining a Bible study group or to check the current arrangements. title: The Church Building
documentTitle: The Church Building | St Michael & All Angels
description: Discover the layers of history in St Michael and All Angels: early stonework, medieval craftsmanship and later changes.
content: ← Visit & Learn Visit & Learn The Church Building Discover the layers of history in St Michael and All Angels: early stonework, medieval craftsmanship and later changes. Early fabric and later change Historic England identifies 10th-century origins, with substantial late-12th-century work. The precise foundation date is uncertain: the parish account’s suggestion of around 950 is an interpretation of early fabric, not a documented building date. The Norman chancel arch, raised in 1872, and the stone font connect the present church with its medieval past. The chancel has narrow lancet windows, but the three east lancets are 19th-century work. The west porch is dated to the 15th century; two medieval grave covers survive inside it. Restoration in 1823 and extensive rebuilding in 1872 changed the church considerably. Our History timeline sets these changes beside the earlier fabric rather than treating the church as an unchanged medieval building. The Norbury Chapel The side chapel dates from around 1300 and has distinctive chequered flint and stone walls. Its chest tomb and brass figures commemorate William Wyddowsoun and his wife. Sources disagree on the memorial’s exact year, so it is described here as early 16th century. The parish’s historical account links the chapel with the Stydolf family and later with the Locks of Norbury, who used it as a family pew. Historic England records 17th-century embossed wooden panels in the chapel. Carving, furnishings and remembrance The elaborately carved wooden pulpit was brought from Belgium in 1840, according to Historic England. The listing also records wooden panels beside the chancel reredos, probably 17th century and brought from Bohemia. Their age is an architectural assessment, not a known carving date. The parish’s historical account dates the present reredos to 1938. It also records the four larger bells given by Dame Elizabeth Lawrence in 1913 in memory of her husband, Sir James Lawrence, completing the peal of six. These details are retained as the account’s record; the bells story includes a link to the historical film. A tradition in the chancel The parish account notes that the chancel is out of alignment with the nave. It traditionally interprets this as a “Weeping Chancel”, evoking Christ’s inclined head on the Cross. This is a symbolic reading of the building; it does not establish why the chancel was built at that angle. title: Eco Church
documentTitle: Eco Church | St Michael & All Angels
description: Care for creation is part of the parish’s life and care for its churchyard. The Eco Group has encouraged practical steps for wildlife, the grounds and church life.
content: ← Visit & Learn About our parish Eco Church Care for creation is part of the parish’s life and care for its churchyard. The Eco Group has encouraged practical steps for wildlife, the grounds and church life. St Michael and All Angels Church viewed across its churchyard. The church and churchyard, pictured in the 2024 Churchyard Trail. “Reducing the causes of climate change is essential to the life of faith. It is a way to love our neighbour and to steward the gift of creation.” The Eco Group was established in 2022 to advise the PCC on local environmental action. The parish registered with the A Rocha Eco Church Award Scheme and received the Eco Church Silver Award. The supplied Churchyard Trail and award badge record this as a 2024 achievement; this page records the award received and does not claim that accreditation is currently active. Practical care for creation Our Eco Journey The parish’s source material records the following work by the Eco Group and volunteers. Hedgerow planting More than 80 metres of hedgerow were planted. The 2024 trail describes newly planted hedges around the newer churchyard as future green corridors for mammals and birds. Churchyard composting The compost area was reorganised so green waste could be composted and the resulting soil returned to areas within the churchyards. A small fruit orchard The Churchyard Trail records that an orchard was planted in winter 2022/23, with apple, pear, damson, quince and medlar trees. Garden of Remembrance Lavender and rosemary were planted around the Garden of Remembrance to provide summer nectar for insects. Wildlife-friendly mowing The trail describes the area behind the church being mown twice a year, and a three-year mowing and raking rotation in the newer churchyard, leaving areas unmown each year. Seasonal pond A rainwater-fed seasonal pond was created in 2024. The trail describes dragonflies, damselflies, pond insects and birds using the area. Information around the churchyard Information boards were installed to explain the changes taking place and why they matter. Reducing harmful chemicals and plastics The Eco Church page and trail describe work to phase out chemical herbicides and pesticides harmful to wildlife, and reduce new or single-use plastics. The trail says churchyard herbicide use had been phased out in favour of a weed burner for paving. Sustainable flower arranging The parish stopped using floral foam and trained flower arrangers to support stems with crumpled chicken wire instead. A living churchyard Churchyard & Wildlife These examples and counts are drawn from the supplied Churchyard Trail (2024) and the earlier Eco Church page. They are records from those sources, not a new survey. Four bat species Serotine, Common Pipistrelle, Soprano Pipistrelle and Brown Long-Eared bats are recorded in the Churchyard Trail. 251 lichen species The 2024 Churchyard Trail says 251 lichen species had been found in the churchyard. Slow worms The trail records slow worms in the churchyard and explains the rotational mowing approach that leaves areas undisturbed. Pond and pollinators The trail describes dragonflies, damselflies and pond insects at the seasonal pond, as well as birds using it. Earlier wildlife records The earlier Eco Church page listed 120 flowering plants and 15 butterfly species in its first-year records; it said records for bees, birds, mammals and reptiles were still to be collated. Lavender around the Garden of Remembrance Flowers for worship and special occasions Creating Beauty, Sustainably For regular and occasional services, the parish encourages seasonal, locally sourced flowers and foliage, and the elimination of floral foam. Flowers are part of many important events; the guidance asks suppliers and arrangers to consider the environmental impact of their materials and the provenance of flowers. The parish asks that floral foam, including the brand Oasis, is not used. title: Philippa Walton
documentTitle: Philippa Walton | St Michael & All Angels
description: Businesswoman, mother and pioneering owner of the Waltham Abbey gunpowder mills, whose family became closely connected with Mickleham.
content: ← People & Families Our History 18th century · People & Families Philippa Walton c. 1674–1749 A pioneering businesswoman whose remarkable life connects the Waltham Abbey gunpowder industry with St Michael & All Angels, Mickleham. A life remembered inside St Michael & All Angels. The marble memorial to Philippa Walton inside St Michael & All Angels, Mickleham Philippa Walton’s memorial inside St Michael & All Angels. Parish/archive photograph supplied for this project. A remarkable woman remembered at Mickleham Inside St Michael & All Angels, an elaborate eighteenth-century monument invites us to remember Philippa Walton. Its words begin with family and friendship. Beyond them lies the story of a woman who carried responsibility for a household and a substantial industrial business. [1] Philippa’s story belongs to two places: the mills at Waltham Abbey and the church at Mickleham, where her son became Rector. The surviving memorial brings that wider history into the space visitors can still enter today. [2] [6] Family, marriage and sudden responsibility Born Philippa Bourchier around 1674, she married William Walton, a London merchant. The monument names her as the daughter and co-heiress of John Bourchier M.D. It remembers ten children and records that six sons and three daughters survived her. [2] [1] William died in 1711. Philippa was left with a young family and the management of his business interests. The monument describes her as “a Young & mournfull Widow”, “Charged with the Care of Ten helpless Infants”. These are the family’s words of remembrance, preserved in stone. [2] [1] Taking charge of the gunpowder mills Philippa took over an enterprise with a London office and production at Balham and Waltham Abbey. Peace in 1713 brought a fall in demand after the War of the Spanish Succession. She closed the Balham operation and concentrated production at Waltham Abbey. [2] In January 1719 she bought three more powder mills and rights to the Mill Stream. Her son John joined in 1723 with a quarter share, becoming an equal partner in 1730. Philippa continued to take an active part in the business. [2] Her achievement was in ownership and management: directing an industrial enterprise through difficult trading conditions. It should not be confused with the physical manufacturing work carried out by the people employed at the mills. [2] The Walton family and Mickleham Philippa’s son, Philip Walton, became Rector of Mickleham in 1745. Westminster School’s archive identifies him as the son of William and Philippa and records his appointment as 6 February 1744/5, using the contemporary double-year date. [6] The British Library’s Hardwicke Papers catalogue also identifies Philip as Rector of Mickleham in records dated 1751–1753. Philippa therefore lived during the early years of her son’s ministry here. Her monument records her death on 7 December 1749. [5] [6] [1] Her memorial at St Michael’s The monument remains a historical object in its own right. Historic England identifies it as an “ashlar and marble rococo wall monument”, with shell features and a swan-neck pediment. [4] Its inscription is also unusually personal. It honours Philippa’s care for her children: she “secured and improved their Property” and “formed their Minds by her Instructions & Example”. These selected words describe both practical responsibility and the family’s affection for her. [1] The monument spells her name PHILLIPA. The article uses Philippa, as in the Royal Gunpowder Mills history. It records her death “in the 74th Year of her Age”; we retain that wording rather than treating it as an exact modern statement of age. In grateful Memory of (the best of Wives, Mothers, and Friends) Mrs PHILLIPA WALTON Daughter and Coheiress of JOHN BOURCHIER M.D. and Relict of WILLIAM WALTON late of LONDON Merchant, (A Gentleman worthy of and happy, in her tenderest Affection.) His early Death left Her a Young & mournfull Widow. Charged with the Care of Ten helpless Infants: Of Whom Six Sons and Three Daughters survived, to Comfort the Life and lament the Death of their Excellent and Amiable Parent; Who, after having secured and improved their Property by her Application & Address, and formed their Minds by her Instructions & Example, retired from the Hurry of Active Life, to end her Days in Piety & Peace. She died (in Calm & Christian Serenity) on the 7th day of December 1749, in the 74th Year of her Age, and is Interred near this Place. An industrial legacy The Walton family continued at Waltham Abbey after Philippa’s death. The Crown bought the mills in 1787; the site became the Royal Gunpowder Mills. title: The Norbury Chapel
documentTitle: The Norbury Chapel | St Michael & All Angels
description: The side chapel, now called the Norbury Chapel, dates from around 1300. Its memorials include the Wyddowsoun tomb and brasses.
content: ← Our History c. 1300 The Norbury Chapel A medieval side chapel with a stone tomb, memorial brasses and connections to Norbury families. The side chapel dates from around 1300. Its chequered flint and stone distinguish it from the surrounding church, giving this small space a character of its own. Inside is the chest tomb of William Wyddowsoun and his wife, with brass figures and an inscription above it. William is remembered as a London citizen and mercer. The tomb’s decorated panels and the figures preserve a personal story within the building’s longer history. Families remembered here The parish account links the chapel to the Stydolf family and, later, to the Locks of Norbury, who used it as a family pew. The memorial belongs to the early 16th century. Sources differ over its exact year, so no single year is given here. Sources & further reading Historic England · chapel and monument British Library · Wyddowsoun brass record ← Back to the timeline Restoration and change →

title: Norman work
documentTitle: Norman work | St Michael & All Angels
description: Much of the present church dates to the Norman period, around 1180, including the chancel arch, lancet windows and font.
content: ← Our History Late 12th century Norman work The Norman chancel arch and font survive within a church much altered in later centuries. Much of the church’s medieval character comes from the late 12th century. Historic England assigns the nave, south aisle, chancel and west tower to that phase, while recording extensive later rebuilding. The chancel arch and font offer particularly clear links with Norman craftsmanship. The arch was raised in 1872: even this early feature tells a story of later change. Look for it in the church The chancel arch. Notice its diamond and dog-tooth decoration at the entrance to the chancel. The stone font. A square bowl with blind arcading stands on a central support and four small columns. The chancel windows. Compare the narrow lancets with their moulded surrounds. The three east lancets are 19th-century work; not every medieval-looking window is medieval. title: Restoration and change
documentTitle: Restoration and change | St Michael & All Angels
description: The church underwent significant alterations: nave arches and piers were replaced in 1823, with further changes during the nineteenth century and the dismantling of the north aisle in 1891.
content: ← Our History 1823–1891 Restoration and change A succession of 19th-century alterations shaped the church we recognise today. The present church brings medieval work and later rebuilding together. The 19th century changed its interior and outline in several stages. 1823 P. F. Robinson restored the church. The parish account records replacement of the nave’s earlier arches and piers. 1842 The parish history records another phase of reconstruction. The extent of this work is less clearly established by the sources consulted. 1872 Historic England records a new north aisle and extensive rebuilding, apart from the tower. The Norman chancel arch was raised. 1891 The parish account describes removal of galleries and further changes to the supports and north aisle. This final phase is retained as that account’s description. These changes help explain why early stonework sits beside later arcades and windows. The dates mark phases of work, rather than a single restoration of an unchanged medieval church. Sources & further reading Historic England · 1823 and 1872 works ← Back to the timeline The bells →

title: Saxon traces
documentTitle: Saxon traces | St Michael & All Angels
description: The original church is thought to have been a small Saxon nave and chancel. Traces of early work remain and may date to around 950.
content: ← Our History 10th-century origins Saxon traces The church has 10th-century origins, but its precise foundation date remains uncertain. The story begins before the Norman Conquest. Historic England identifies 10th-century origins, while describing the surviving west doorway more cautiously as probably of that period. The parish history suggests a date around 950 for early work. This is an interpretation, not a documented foundation or construction date. The church recorded in Domesday in 1086 gives us a firmer point in the story. An early trace The tall, narrow west doorway is described as probably 10th century. Its dating remains an architectural judgement. title: A Harvest of Thankfulness
documentTitle: A Harvest of Thankfulness | News | St Michael & All Angels
description: Flowers, worship, food and fellowship filled St Michael's as our church family gathered to celebrate Harvest together.
content: ← Back to News Harvest Family Service A Harvest of Thankfulness Sunday 4 October 2026 The Harvest congregation seen from the gallery, looking towards the altar Autumn arrived beautifully at St Michael's this Sunday, with the church filled with flowers, pumpkins and the rich colours of the season for our Harvest Family Service. Harvest has long been a time when Christians give thanks for the gifts of the earth and for all those whose work helps to bring food to our tables. But our celebration this year also invited us to think a little more deeply about what having food means in different parts of the world. Sunflowers, hydrangeas and autumn foliage arranged inside the church The altar frontal reads Praise God for Harvest beneath the carved reredos During the service, we reflected on the enormous variety of food enjoyed across different countries and cultures. At the same time, we remembered that for many people a full table cannot be taken for granted. In countries affected by war and conflict, families may face uncertainty not only about tomorrow, but about something as simple as their next meal. That reflection gave an important meaning to our Harvest celebration. Giving thanks for what we have also encourages us to remember others, and reminds us that gratitude and generosity belong together. A Harvest reflection at the front of the congregation with a basket of produce There was plenty of joy too. Our younger members helped bring the Family Service to life, while the beautiful Harvest decorations throughout the church provided a wonderful backdrop to our worship. Two children and an adult share their colourful Harvest crafts After the service, the celebration continued with food, conversation and time together. People gathered around the table, caught up with friends and neighbours, and enjoyed the warmth of being together as a church community. Members of the parish beside the table of food after the Harvest service Children and adults share food and conversation after worship It was a lovely Harvest Sunday in Mickleham — a chance to worship, to give thanks, to think of others and simply to enjoy one another's company. Thank you to everyone who decorated the church, contributed to the service, prepared and shared food, and helped make the day so special. description: This is the Data Privacy Notice of the Parochial Church Council (PCC) of St. Michael and All Angels Church, Mickleham.
content: ← About our parish Privacy & GDPR Privacy & GDPR This is the Data Privacy Notice of the Parochial Church Council (PCC) of St. Michael and All Angels Church, Mickleham. Data Privacy Consent Form General Data Protection Regulation Data Privacy Notice The Parochial Church Council (PCC) of St. Michael and All Angels Church, Mickleham (St. Michael’s) 1. Your personal data - what is it? Personal data relates to a living individual who can be identified from that data (for example a name, address, email address, photographs or videos). Identification can be by the information alone or in conjunction with any other information in the data controller’s possession or likely to come into such possession. The processing of personal data is governed by the General Data Protection Regulation (“the GDPR”). 2. Who are we? The PCC of St. Michael’s is the data controller (contact details below). This means it decides how your personal data is processed and for what purposes. 3. How do we process your personal data? The PCC of St. Michael’s complies with its obligations under the GDPR by keeping personal data up to date; by storing and destroying it securely; by not collecting or retaining excessive amounts of data; by protecting personal data from loss, misuse, unauthorised access and disclosure and by ensuring that appropriate technical measures are in place to protect personal data. We use your personal data for the following purposes: To enable us to meet all legal, contractual and statutory obligations (which include maintaining and publishing our Electoral Roll in accordance with the Church Representation Rules). To carry out comprehensive safeguarding procedures (including due diligence and complaints handling) in accordance with best safeguarding practice from time to time with the aim of ensuring that all children and adults-at-risk are provided with safe environments. To enable us to provide a voluntary service for the benefit of the public in a particular geographical area as specified in our constitution. To administer membership records. To fundraise and promote the interests of the charity. To manage our employees and volunteers. To maintain our own accounts and records (including the processing of Gift Aid applications). To inform you of news, events, activities and services running at St. Michael’s. To share your contact details with the Diocesan office so they can keep you informed about news in the Diocese and events, activities and services that will be occurring in the Diocese and in which you may be interested. 4. What is the legal basis for processing your personal data? Explicit consent of the data subject so that we can keep you informed about news, events, activities and services and keep you informed about diocesan events. Processing is necessary for carrying out legal and contractual obligations in relation to Gift Aid. Processing is carried out by a not-for-profit body with a religious aim provided: the processing relates only to members or former members (or those who have regular contact with it in connection with those purposes), and there is no disclosure to a third party without consent. 5. Sharing your personal data Your personal data will be treated as strictly confidential and will only be shared with other members of the church in order to carry out a service to other church members or for purposes connected with the church. We will only share your data with third parties outside the parish with your consent. 6. How long do we keep your personal data? 1 We keep data in accordance with the guidance set out in the guide “Keep or Bin: Care of Your Parish Records” which is available from the Church of England website [see footnote for link]. Specifically, we retain electoral roll data while it is still current; Gift Aid declarations and associated paperwork for up to 6 years after the calendar year to which they relate; financial records for a minimum period of 7 years to support HMRC audits; Charity Commission audits and parish registers (baptisms, marriages, funerals) permanently. 7. Your rights and your personal data Unless subject to an exemption under the GDPR, you have the following rights with respect to your personal data: The right to request a copy of your personal data which the PCC of St. Michael’s holds about you. The right to request that the PCC of St. Michael’s corrects any personal data if it is found to be inaccurate or out of date. The right to request your personal data is erased where it is no longer necessary for the PCC of St. Michael’s to retain such data. The right to withdraw your consent to the processing at any time. The right to request that the data controller provide the data subject with his/her personal data and where possible, to transmit that data directly to another data controller, (known as the right to data portability), (where applicable). The right, where there is a dispute in relation to the accuracy or processing of your personal data, to request a restriction is placed on further processing. The right to object to the processing of personal data, (where applicable). The right to lodge a complaint with the Information Commissioners Office. 8. Further processing If we wish to use your personal data for a new purpose, not covered by this Data Protection Notice, then we will provide you with a new notice explaining this new use prior to commencing the processing and setting out the relevant purposes and processing conditions. Where and whenever necessary, we will seek your prior consent to the new processing. A form for your preferences Data Privacy Consent Form Use this form to tell St. Michael and All Angels Church which contact methods and information-processing purposes you consent to, as described in the form. Download Data Privacy Consent Form (PDF) 9. Contact Details To exercise all relevant rights, queries or complaints please in the first instance contact: The data controller The Data Controller, the PCC of St. Michael’s Email admin@micklehamchurch.org.uk Telephone 01372 376443 St. Michael and All Angels Church Old London Road Mickleham Surrey RH5 6DU Information Commissioner’s Office You can contact the Information Commissioners Office on 0303 123 1113 or via email https://ico.org.uk/global/contact-us/email/ or at the Information Commissioner's Office, Wycliffe House, Water Lane, Wilmslow, Cheshire. SK9 5AF. Details about retention periods can currently be found in the Record Management Guides located on the Church of England website at: https://www.churchofengland.org/more/libraries-and-archives/records-management-guides Back to About our parish

The Parochial Church Council (PCC) of St. Michael and All Angels Church, Mickleham (St. Michael’s) Our safeguarding commitments This policy statement actively underpins all safeguarding work within the church. In accordance with the Church of England Safeguarding Policy our church is committed to: Promoting a safer environment and culture Safely recruiting and supporting all those with any responsibility related to children, young people and vulnerable adults within the church Responding promptly to every safeguarding concern or allegation Caring pastorally for any victims/survivors of abuse and other affected persons Caring pastorally for those who are the subject of concerns or allegations of abuse and other affected persons Responding to those who may present a risk to others How the parish keeps people safe The parish will: Create a safe and caring place for all Have a named Parish Safeguarding Officer (PSO) to work with the incumbent and the PCC to implement policy and procedures Safely recruit, train and support all those with any responsibility for children, young people and adults to have the confidence and skills to recognise and respond to abuse Ensure that there is Discover their story William Mowsurth · 1507–1513 Historical photograph associated with William Mowsurth Rector · 1507–1513 William Mowsurth Their story William Mowfurth was a late-medieval English priest whose ministry connected Mickleham with several Surrey parishes in the years immediately before the Reformation. Historical records identify him as Rector of Puttenham, Mickleham and Streatham. He died in 1513. Mowfurth appears to have held more than one parish living, a practice that was possible among clergy of his period. His connection with Streatham can be traced to at least 1492, when he appears in the historical list of Rectors of St Leonard's Church. His period as Rector of Mickleham is traditionally recorded as 1507–1513, although the precise starting date at Mickleham still requires confirmation from the original ecclesiastical records. Remarkably, a physical memorial to Mowfurth has survived for more than five centuries. His monumental brass is preserved at St Leonard's Church, Streatham. It depicts him as a priest in Mass vestments, with his hands joined in prayer, standing above a Latin memorial inscription. Historic England records the brass among the significant monuments in the chancel of St Leonard's and dates it to 1513. The survival of the brass is particularly valuable because it gives us something much more personal than a name in a list of Rectors: it allows us to see how William Mowfurth chose to be commemorated at the end of his life. The priestly vestments and prayerful pose place him unmistakably within the religious world of England before the Reformation. He died more than twenty years before Henry VIII's break with Rome and therefore ministered to Mickleham when its worship was still part of the medieval Western Church. Mowfurth's memorial was important enough to attract the attention of later antiquarians. The British Library preserves a rubbing of the brass in the collection of Alfred Ridley Bax, catalogued as a rubbing of William Mowfurth, Rector of Streatham and Mickelham, at Streatham, 1513. A second British Library catalogue record also identifies a sepulchral brass of William Mowfurth at Streatham dated 1513. His connection with Mickleham is therefore not based solely upon later local tradition. It is independently recorded by the British Library, while the general index to the Surrey Archaeological Collections describes William Mowfurth specifically as Rector of Puttenham, Mickleham and Streatham and directs readers to a discussion of his brass in volume 32, pages 125–127. An old image preserved at Mickleham records him as “Wm. Mowsurth, Rector; d. 1513”, with a later handwritten annotation, “Rector of Mickleham 1507–1513.” The spelling of his surname varies in historical material, but modern archival catalogues generally use Mowfurth. William Mowfurth therefore provides a rare tangible link with Mickleham's pre-Reformation history. More than five hundred years after his death, his memorial survives at Streatham, historical rubbings of it survive in the British Library, and an old representation preserved at Mickleham continues to connect his story with the parish he once served. Sources & further reading Surrey Archaeological Collections, Vol. 32, pp. 125–127 Surrey Archaeological Collections, Vol. 32, pp. 125–127 — the Society's general index explicitly identifies “Mowfurth, William, Rector of Puttenham, Mickleham and Streatham, his brass” and points to those pages. This is probably our most useful historical secondary source. View source British Library, Add MS 39794 HH, item 8 British Library, Add MS 39794 HH, item 8 — catalogued as “William Mowfurth, Rector of Streatham and Mickelham: Rubbing of brass of, at Streatham: 1513.” This is excellent independent evidence for his connection with Mickleham. View source British Library, Add MS 32490 Y, item 14 British Library, Add MS 32490 Y, item 14 — another archival record of the sepulchral brass of William Mowfurth, Rector of Streatham, 1513. View source Historic England, List Entry 1100267 Historic England, List Entry 1100267 – Church of St Leonard, Streatham — the official listing records a brass to William Mowfurth, d.1513, in the chancel. View source St Leonard's Church, Streatham – parish history St Leonard's Church, Streatham – parish history — its own history identifies William Mowfurth (1492) as one of its Rectors and says that he is commemorated by a brass in the sanctuary. Mowsurth, Rector; d.1513”, with the handwritten annotation “Rector of Mickleham 1507–1513.” I'd catalogue this as local archival evidence, rather than treating the handwritten 1507 date as independently proven. George Lock · 1796–1800 Historical photograph associated with George Lock Curate · 1796–1800 George Lock Their story George Lock (1771–1864) belonged to the Lock family of Norbury Park, Mickleham. He was the son of William Lock and Frederica Augusta Schaub, and studied at Christ Church, Oxford, gaining his BA in 1794 and MA in 1796. A published account of Fanny Burney’s connections with Mickleham identifies George as a curate at St Michael’s, where his family worshipped. His exact dates of service remain to be confirmed. He later became rector of St Margaret’s, Lee, Kent, serving from 1803 until his death on 17 November 1864. His long ministry encompassed the rebuilding of the parish church twice, culminating in the present building, consecrated in 1841. In 1814, George and 39 inhabitants of Lee signed a petition urging Parliament to act against the continuation of the African slave trade. Portraits of him survive in the National Portrait Gallery, and a memorial cross commemorates him at St Margaret’s. Sources & further reading Miriam Al Jamil, “Fanny Burney and Mickleham,” Burney Letter, Vol. 20, No. 2, autumn 2014. Identifies George, William Lock’s younger son, as a curate at St Michael’s, where the Lock family worshipped. View source Joseph Foster, Alumni Oxonienses, entry for George Lock. During his Mickleham incumbency he also became Rector of St James’s Piccadilly in 1802 and Dean of Canterbury in 1809. Did you know? He was offered the Bishopric of Chester in 1812 and declined it. Canon John Harkin B.A. Their story John Harkin served Mickleham during two separate periods: 1993–1998 and 2018–2020. Appointment reporting from 1998 identifies him as Priest-in-Charge of Mickleham and Chaplain of Box Hill School when he left for Jersey. Parish material from 2018 describes his return after twenty years. Rev. Barbara Steadman-Allen B.Mus. · 1999–2004 Historical photograph associated with Rev. Barbara Steadman-Allen B.Mus. When Leatherhead and Mickleham entered a new benefice arrangement in 2002, she continued as the priest responsible for Mickleham while the parishes retained their own PCCs and identities. Rev. David Ireland M.A. (Oxon) · 2005–2012 Historical photograph associated with Rev. David Ireland M.A. (Oxon) Parish clergy · 2005–2012 Rev. title: Mickleham War Memorial
documentTitle: Mickleham War Memorial | St Michael & All Angels
description: The war memorial stands in the churchyard at St Michael & All Angels and commemorates local people who died in the two world wars.
content: Mickleham War Memorial stone cross and stepped base, with St Michael & All Angels Church behind it. ← Visit & Learn Local History Mickleham War Memorial The war memorial stands in the churchyard at St Michael & All Angels and commemorates local people who died in the two world wars. A lasting tribute The inscription records that this cross was erected in 1920 by the parish of Mickleham, “to the glory of God and in memory of” those commemorated here. Its stepped stone base bears names alongside the words “Who fell in the Great War 1914–1919”. These inscriptions connect the memorial with the people remembered after the First World War. The memorial also commemorates the Second World War. Another face reads “This cross is also in memory of”, above further names, with the dates 1939–1945 engraved on the base. Standing beside St Michael & All Angels, it is a place to pause and remember. The parish calendar includes an Act of Remembrance at the War Memorial, keeping remembrance part of parish life today.
